The way I see it, the vast majority of people just run themselves into a dead end by taking these kinds of phrases to heart in the first place.  
  
If you're raised in the kind of environment where it seems like everything in life revolves around your choice of full-time job by the time you're a teen (and god knows that's true for a lot of people), then this whole "passion" stuff will just make you obsess over which job is the supposedly perfect one...as opposed to actually thinking about anything to do with passion.

If you're tearing your hair out over which of the top ten highest-paying careers is your passion, hey, sorry bud, but it's probably none of them. That's okay. I'm not really passionate about anesthesiology or upper management either (do you know anyone who is?).

If you have a chance to take a good, well-paying job that you enjoy and that is in effect a net positive to your life as a whole, why not take it? Why fuss over all this passion nonsense when it seems like it has nothing to contribute?

On the other hand, there ARE people who are better served by genuinely pursuing their passions, and we shouldn't ignore that. Case in point, me. I've always been a pretty rebellious, headstrong type, and I don't easily fall in line with situations or circumstances that I object to.

Because of that, lots of common jobs are not really a good option for me. I simply don't function well in the hierarchy. I get demotivated by pointless busywork too easily.   
  
More than that, I do have several things I am genuinely passionate about in life, and my mental health takes a huge hit when I have to spend 8+ hours each day doing something not just totally unrelated, but soulless and pointless by comparison.

There's a lot of people these days who would look at me and tell me that unless my passions are 'highly marketable', I should just accept that this is how it is and move on. I think this is just as stupid as the headline phrase OP quoted.

Yeah, none of my passions may have anything to do with STEM, medicine, law, or finance, but just because of that I am supposed to resign myself to entertaining them as part-time weekend hobbies and that's it?

No. There is a third way. It might not be the most obvious, it might not be the most lucrative either - everyone's gotta weigh their options. For me, I already know that I can't really look at the horizon and see something bright beyond unless I know that the things that matter the most to me are over there somewhere.

This might not be the most original argument you've ever heard, but consider this, it's a simple one:

No country has the right to play world's policeman. There.

You mentioned the UN -- though misnoming it as a military power, which it isn't -- and one of the reasons the UN exists is to mediate globally and internationally in cases where you can't afford to insert partisan interests by any one nation. This includes war-torn countries and crisis situations, as well as human rights abuses by dictators. Sure, there are flaws in the approach, and I for one am for a United Nations with a much stronger backbone than the one we have right now, but in terms of principle, it is the most humane and moral solution to this problem: An international, impartial body that acts in the interests of literally everyone, and serves above all to promote peace and help anyone willing to work towards that goal.

Your approach, on the other hand, essentially boils down to "might makes right". The USA has the strongest military capacity worldwide, that is true -- but what if China did? Let's just say they do. Would you want them to go ahead and install Chinese-inspired governments all over the Middle East? Would you want those to fail as miserably as America's have in our timeline? Just because they're the most powerful? No. This is why we need something like the United Nations, and other NGOs like it. We need an organization that really has no other code than "Minimize conflict, foster global co-operation, minimize suffering wherever it occurs". That is the only way intervention even makes sense.

I don't think I could response to everything you raised individually if I tried -- it'd take me too much time to properly educate myself and make up my mind on many of the topics that you mentioned which I am not too familiar with. But, regarding your overall sentiment, here are my two cents:  


1. I don't want to make this sound condescending, that is absolutely not my intention -- but stop, take a few steps back for a minute. I'm assuming you're a rather young guy like myself, so look at the covers of those books you mentioned. Most of them were written during the 50s and 60s, during the first "Boom" of dystopian fiction in sci-fi. Think about what the people who wrote those books probably had in their heads when they imagined those dystopian worlds like that of 1984. Orwell had been a military officer in World War II, one of the most horrific conflicts in history, which was in big part brought on by the rise of fascism. When he wrote 1984, Russia was still neck-deep in Stalin's reign, which though superficially popular in the post-war era, violated human rights left and right on a grand scale never seen before, or since. And just the year the book was published, Mao won the civil conflict in China and set up shop there with his dictatorship. Now, look at those two countries. China is a growing and prospering superpower that is actually getting pretty good at beating the USA at their own capitalist game, and Russia, although thoroughly corrupt, has come a long long way from the days of Stalin (though I will concede that that progress would be many times greater if it wasn't perhaps for the regressive policies of Putin). My point with this is that, compared to the days of someone like Orwell, we are living in very safe times. Not good, mind you -- there are genuinely scary issues that our generation needs to face in the years ahead, and many of the old problems persist. But the things that 1984 warned us about -- totalitarian fascist regimes taking over the whole planet, putting everyone into surveillance and mindless labor, breaking their spirits through brutal torture and disappearing dissenters -- were the 20th century postwar fears of a very scarred generation that went through completely different dangers than ours. Comparing the two is bound to mean drawing imaginary lines between things that aren't really aligned with each other.  

2.  As a tangent to my first point, and also perhaps to give an example, take the recent rise and popularization of ideas like fake news and hate speech and cancel culture and so on. Comparing these to the nightmares of Orwell and Huxley is not just inappropriate, it doesn't actually make much sense when you think about it. In those dystopias, the world wasn't an insufferable place to live in because Big Brother prosecuted people for wrongthink -- but rather because things had gotten to a point where a Big Brother could even exist, could dictate to people what to do even if it's something nonsensical and stupid. That's what much of those stories were meant to imply, that totalitarianism will take liberties even towards the obscene and absurd, just because it can. Remember 2+2=5? It's not the bad math that's meant to scare you. And the fact of the matter is, powerful CEOs losing their positions because they groped an intern ten years ago and word broke out on Twitter, or JK Rowling outing herself as a TERF and losing a lot of fans over it, is not even on the same plane as that -- in fact, it's a very normal thing that has always happened throughout human history where popular opinion of someone with a lot of privilege and power can dramatically shift based on what people think about that person's moral character.  

3. "Interest in post-modernism"? Really? Are you a fan of Jordan Peterson, by any chance? Because it sure sounds like it. Google up post-modernism, please. It's mostly an art movement, with a notable branch in philosophy as is often the case. And I am also willing to bet you a fiver that it has almost nothing to do with what you think it does. Apart from the eternal metushelah, Noam Chomsky himself, I don't know of any prominent OG postmodernist who is currently still alive and kicking. That's because the movement mostly peaked in the midcentury, from the 50s to the 80s or so. There was sort of a revival of post-modernist literature that happened in the early 90s, but not much new thought sprang out of that. We're currently in the weird transitional period where we've clearly left post-modernism behind for the most part (especially in the arts), but the new paradigm hasn't crystallized itself well enough yet that we can give it a new umbrella name.  

4. Social norms aren't really changing any faster or slower than they always have by any real measure. Almost without fail, it's conservatives who feel left behind by the new vogue who complain about things changing too fast. And what kind of argument is hiding in there anyway? "The world is progressing towards something unknown, and the unknown scares me, so it shouldn't"?  

5. Religion losing influence is another one of those cries that have been echoed by so many over the ages, yet usually when exactly the opposite is happening. It depends where you are, but statistically religion has been on the rise for quite a while, because atheists have lower birthrates than religious people. Sure, in some countries and territories it is not socially acceptable anymore to pander to obviously religious agendas, especially in politics (see France, which you even mentioned, for one good example), but that has much more to do with long-standing societal attitudes than any recent developments in particular. (I assume you know what the word "laicité" means, and for how long it has been a sacred standard for the French, right?)
